title: Poor or rich (Avot 4:9)
hook: a gym habit that only lasts while life is easy: Yonatan says keep Torah in poverty and you'll keep it in wealth
tomorrow: too busy to breathe. what does Rabbi Meir say to cut?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Ishmael: don't judge alone, and don't say accept my view. Only One judges alone. Now, a harder week.

Does the practice go when the money goes? It's often the first thing to go: the class, the lessons, the long run, the habit that only lived while life was easy. Then the budget comes back, and the habit doesn't. Rabbi Yonatan has a line about exactly that, and on first hearing it seems backwards. Keep it when you're poor, he says, and you'll keep it when you're rich. Why would hard times come first?
screen: `THE MONEY GOES.` → `THE HABIT GOES TOO.` → `WHY DOES POOR COME FIRST?`

segments.voice: Here's the whole saying, in plain words. Whoever keeps the Torah in poverty will in the end keep it in wealth. And whoever neglects the Torah in wealth will in the end neglect it in poverty. Now the odd detail. You'd expect a promise about money: be faithful when broke and you'll get rich. Some readers do hear it that way. But look at what actually carries across the line. Not the money. The keeping. Each half is a forecast about a habit. What you do with the Torah on a thin week is what you'll do with it on a full one. And the second half closes the escape hatch. Plenty is not a better time to start. Whoever lets it slide when they have everything will let it slide when they have nothing, too. Some readers take poverty and wealth more widely than a bank balance. Poor in time, rich in time. Poor in energy, rich in spare hours. Either way, the puzzle solves itself the same way: hard times come first because that's where the habit is actually built. A practice that only survives easy weeks was never really yours. One that survived a hard week will still be there when things open up. Poor or rich, it's the same practice.
screen: `KEEP IT POOR, KEEP IT RICH.` · `NEGLECT IT RICH, NEGLECT IT POOR.` · `IT'S A FORECAST ABOUT A HABIT.` · `HARD WEEKS BUILD IT.` · then, large: `POOR OR RICH.`

segments.voice: Choose one practice you keep, or mean to keep: a few minutes of study, a blessing before you eat, this lesson. Name the hard week that would most likely knock it out. Then make a plan for the smallest version that could survive that week, one minute, one line, one breath, and say it to yourself once: when that week comes, I'll do the small version.
screen: `ONE PRACTICE.` · `THE WEEK THAT BREAKS IT.` · `THE SMALLEST VERSION THAT SURVIVES.`

segments.voice: Poor or rich. Rabbi Yonatan's saying: keep the Torah in a hard time and you'll keep it in a good one.
For the road: poor or rich, the same practice, built on the thin weeks. That's day thirty-one of sixty.

howItsDone: Many Jews keep a fixed time for study, even a few minutes a day, and the custom is to keep it in busy or lean seasons as well as easy ones.
